meta.title: Two contractor workers drowned at an overflowing return-water dam (facilitator answer)
meta.location: North return-water dam and pump installation
meta.client: Training case study (anonymised; based on a real event)
meta.description: After heavy rain higher up in the catchment, the mine's north return-water dam rose quickly and began to overflow. The mine became aware of the rising level too late, and the pump installation at the dam was being flooded. The engineering manager asked the owner of a small contracting company working on site to help save the pumps. The contractor and two of his workers, none of whom had done work on water before, took an old boat that had been stored on site unused for many years to reach the flooded equipment, with one person on the bank holding a line. The current and wind pushed the boat away faster than the shore attendant could hold it, and it drifted towards the high overflow. Afraid of being carried over the wall, the two workers left the boat to reach the bank. Neither could swim; they underestimated the distance to the dam side and their work clothes and boots hampered them. Both drowned. There was no pre-task risk assessment or job plan, no life jackets or rescue equipment at the dam, and the workers had no training for work on or near water, water rescue or first aid for drowning.
meta.summary: Four trios describe the event: the catchment flood overflows the dam and floods the pumps; the decision to recover the pumps puts an old boat with two inexperienced contractor workers on the overflowing dam; the boat drifts towards the spillway and the workers leave it; and, with no life-saving equipment, swimming ability or rescue capability, both drown. Six barriers failed and seven were missing or inadequate. The Underlying Causes sit in flood defences and dam procedures, competing goals in an emergency, a contractor management process so cumbersome that managers routinely bypass it, uncontrolled disused equipment, and the absence of any requirement, training or equipment for work on or near water.
meta.lessons:
In a flood emergency, stop work on or near the water; protect people before equipment.
A slow contractor process does not stop contractors being used: it pushes the work outside the process.
Work on or near water needs a plan, life jackets, a rescue capability and people who have been trained, every time.
Disused equipment left on site will be used: remove it or control it.

actions.text: Subscribe the control room to the weather service and upstream gauge alerts for the dam catchment; set level and rainfall trigger alarms and test them monthly.
Raise or flood-protect the pump installation above the assessed maximum flood level, or fit remote isolation so nobody needs to approach it in a flood.
Add a "stop work on or near the dam" rule and spillway exclusion zone to the dam flood procedure; brief all supervisors and the control room.
Contractors may only start work covered by an approved scope; any new task needs a scope variation signed by the contract owner and SHE before work starts.
Require a written task risk assessment and job plan, approved by the responsible supervisor, before any work on or near water, including emergencies.
Remove the old boat from site; any boat used on site must be registered, inspected before each use and fit for the water conditions.
Define shore-control requirements for boat work (anchored line, winch or second boat, maximum wind and flow) in the water-work standard.
Include "stay with the boat, signal and wait for rescue" in the pre-task briefing and in the water-work training.
Issue certified life jackets for all work on or near water and make wearing them a condition of access to the dam water edge.
Specify PPE for work on water (life jacket, light footwear) in the PPE matrix and the water-work standard.
Install rescue points (ring buoy and throw line) at every dam access point and inspect them monthly.
Train the dam area first aiders and emergency team in drowning first aid (rescue breathing and CPR) and refresh it yearly.
Install a rain gauge and upstream level sensor in the upper catchment with telemetry to the control room.
Revise the dam operating procedure with flood trigger levels, actions per level and who is called; exercise it before the next rainy season.
Include maximum flood levels in the design review checklist for all installations at dams and water courses.
Add "people before equipment" decision rules to the emergency management procedure and brief all managers.
Review the contractor management process with users; introduce a fast-track route for urgent work that still checks scope, competence and risk; monitor out-of-scope requests monthly.
Check contractor competence for each new task type against the task requirements before approval, and keep the record.
Introduce a one-page quick risk assessment for emergency and unplanned work, with a required second signature.
Survey the site for disused equipment and either remove it or tag it out of service in a register; repeat yearly.
Write an emergency procedure for a boat in distress and for persons in the water, and brief it to everyone working on water.
Introduce water-safety training with a swimming-ability check for anyone who works on or near water.
Write a site standard for work on or near water that requires life jackets, rescue equipment and a rescuer for every task.
Review the PPE matrix for all water-related tasks and update it.
Add water rescue scenarios to the emergency response plan and hold a water rescue drill at the dam within six months.
Add drowning to the first-aid training content and the site first-aid procedure.

evidence.narrative:
On the afternoon of 14 February, after heavy rain higher up in the catchment, the north return-water dam rose fast and started to overflow. As far as I can tell the control room only noticed when the pump installation was already being flooded; I assume there was no warning from upstream. The engineering manager phoned the owner of the civils contractor who was on site for other work and asked him to help get the pumps out. I believe this was a one-off request in the emergency, but contractors here are often asked to do odd jobs outside their scope because the contractor process is slow.

The contractor and two of his workers used an old aluminium boat that had been lying behind the pump station for years. Nobody I spoke to knows when it was last used or checked. One worker stayed on the bank holding a rope tied to the boat. The shore attendant says the current and the wind pushed the boat towards the spillway and the rope was pulled out of his hands. The two in the boat probably panicked when they saw they were heading for the overflow wall, and they went into the water to swim to the bank. Neither could swim. I think they misjudged the distance to the bank, which looks like 15 to 20 m, and their overalls and safety boots would have dragged them down. There were no life jackets, ring buoys or throw lines at the dam. Nobody did a risk assessment or planned the job, and as far as we know none of them had any training for working on water, rescue or first aid for drowning.

What we do not have yet: drawings of the dam with depths and levels, the spillway height, the positions of the boat and the people, the time line of the alarm and the phone calls, and the wind direction and speed at the time.
evidence.notes: The scene changes fast once the dam level drops: survey the water line, the debris line and the boat position first. Secure the control room level records, phone records and any CCTV today. Interview the shore attendant, the contractor owner and the engineering manager separately and as soon as possible, and record the time line before anything else.
